chunks: "Efficiency is output power divided by input power, so it tells you what fraction of the energy you take from the source actually gets to the load.
The rest, input minus output, is loss, and it all turns into heat.
To measure it, I measure four things at the same time: input voltage and current, and output voltage and current, then compute Vout times Iout over Vin times Iin.
On the bench that's two or four multimeters, or a power analyzer, with an electronic load on the output.
I'd sense the voltages right at the converter's pins with separate sense leads, because the drop in the leads can be a percent or two.
I'd let it warm up to steady state, and I'd sweep the load from very light to full and repeat at the minimum, nominal and maximum input voltage, because efficiency is a curve, not a number.
For switching converters where ripple matters, I use true-RMS or averaging meters or a scope with math for the average of v times i.
It matters for heat: at 10 watts out, 90 percent means 1. 1 watts of loss, 70 percent is 4. 3 watts.
It also sets battery life, size and cost of the thermal solution, and reliability, since temperature drives failures. For some products it's a regulatory number as well."
